source.title: Tracing Facts or just Copies? A critical investigation of the Competitions of Mechanisms in Large Language Models
source.authors: Dante Campregher; Yanxu Chen; S. Hoffman; Maria Heuss

page_placements.theme: Copy-suppression and copying heads in the competition between in-context text and stored facts

record.tranche_reason: The study tests the copy-suppression interpretation using attention-score scaling and factual/counterfactual output measures, rather than directly reproducing the original circuit and loss-attribution analysis.
record.gate_note: The study tests whether strengthening heads that promote factual answers also suppresses a factual token when it is already present in the prompt. It does not measure L10H7's exact attention destination or logit effect on the training distribution, and does not test calibration, self-repair, or the 76.9% loss figure. Some results are reported only in figures; the text gives thresholds for the factual-prompt experiment but does not resolve those outcomes by individual head. Prompt-structure and premise robustness results concern the factual-versus-counterfactual competition, not the same-token copying behavior, and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses attention-score amplification on CounterFact-derived prompts to test whether GPT-2's factual-promoting heads (L10H7 with L11H10) and Pythia-6.9B's analogues act as general copy suppressors. When the prompt states the true fact and the heads are amplified, they suppress that fact. This bears directly on V1 and on V5 for the Pythia part. It does not reproduce the original QK/OV or loss analysis.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that factual-promoting heads act through general copy suppression (anti-induction) rather than selective counterfactual suppression, because amplifying them also suppresses facts stated in the prompt. They find head contributions are domain-dependent, more so in Pythia-6.9B, and say more model sizes are needed to confirm the size effect.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses attention-score modification and factual-versus-counterfactual output rates on CounterFact-derived prompts; it does not reproduce the original study's QK/OV circuit and loss-contribution analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The factual/counterfactual outcome varies with alpha; the best alpha depends on sentence-structure matching in the robustness experiments. Head contributions also vary by answer category, and the study reports more pronounced category-dependent patterns in Pythia-6.9B than GPT-2.

fits_no_version.finding: In GPT-2 with boosted heads (alpha 10), factual output is 71% when the fact appears in the subject but 23% when it does not; 45% of no-hint outputs are neither target.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Boosting factual-promoting heads raises factual output mainly when the fact can be copied from context, not through factual recall.

record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the main factual-prompt output rates. The text does not resolve those results by individual head, uses CounterFact-derived prompts rather than the training distribution, and reports some category results only in figures. The authors themselves note that more model sizes within one model family would be needed to confirm the size-specialization result.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the many premise and sentence-structure conditions in Sections 4.2.1–4.2.2 and Table 1 because they report factual-versus-counterfactual competition, not the same-token copying behavior. Omitted no-hint Pythia factual-recall rates because the factual token is not present earlier in those prompts. Other head-category plots in Figures 7–13 were not entered because they concern heads other than GPT-2 L10H7 or do not report the L10H7 copy-suppression behavior.

untested.parts: The training distribution; the unamplified (natural) behaviour; attention to the earlier occurrence; whether earlier components predict the token; isolating L10H7 from L11H10.
The QK/OV circuit analysis and the share of loss explained (76.9%).
IOI negative name movers; any mechanistic comparison showing that the Pythia heads share L10H7's QK/OV mechanism; other model sizes.

missing.what: GPT-2 counterfactual-prompt result: amplifying L10H7 and L11H10 attention to the earlier counterfactual token raises factual output from 65/10000 (alpha 0) to 5032 (alpha 5) and 5274 (alpha 10), i.e. it suppresses copying of the present token. The record excluded this as 'competition, not copying', but it is copy suppression of a token present earlier.
Pythia-6.9B category dependence: L20H18 has negligible effect on some categories, and SVD shows domain-specific encoded tokens.

record.verdict_notes: All evidence comes from amplified attention (alpha≥5), not from natural behaviour, and heads are modified jointly, so L10H7's own share cannot be separated. The reader's 'supports' label from r7 was removed: r7 is a control on different prompts, not a test of V1. The study cites McDougall et al. (the original) but is not itself an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses CounterFact-derived prompts, not the training distribution; it does not directly establish that earlier components predict the token, measure attention to the earlier occurrence, or isolate L10H7 from the other head of interest in the factual-prompt result.
The study does not analyze L10H7's QK or OV circuit or measure its share of loss, including the 76.9% figure.
Calibration and overconfidence are not measured.
Self-repair and upstream-copier ablation are not tested.
The study tests a copy-suppression-like effect in Pythia-6.9B, but does not test negative name movers in IOI or establish that those heads and L10H7 share the same mechanism across tasks and models.
The study does not measure self-repair or compare its sources.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Scaled the attention score for the head or heads of interest when the prompt stated the factual token and then repeated the factual sentence.

conditions.value: CounterFact-derived prompts with counterfactual targets replaced by factual targets

rows.measure: Proportion of outputs predicting the factual token
rows.note: The authors say the factual-response proportion steadily decreases as alpha increases. The result is not resolved by individual head in the text.
rows.check: The subject is GPT-2 L10H7 and L11H10 modified jointly, not L10H7 alone. The alpha=0 baseline is only in Figure 5 and not stated. A drop to below 90% at alpha=5 is a moderate suppression of the stated factual token.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Scaled the attention score for the head or heads of interest when the prompt stated the factual token and then repeated the factual sentence.

conditions.value: CounterFact-derived prompts with counterfactual targets replaced by factual targets

rows.measure: Proportion of outputs predicting the factual token
rows.note: The authors report that strengthening the head or heads reduces factual predictions even though the fact appears in the prompt. The text does not give a head-specific value.
rows.check: The subject is L10H7 and L11H10 jointly. The value is an upper bound (<70%), and the baseline is figure-only. Suppression of a token already present in the context is clearly shown under amplification.

rows.subject: Pythia-6.9B

rows.note: The study reports the effect for the attention heads of interest, without giving a head-specific value.
rows.check: The subject is Pythia-6.9B heads L17H28, L20H18 and L21H8 modified jointly. The value is a bound (<70%) and the baseline is figure-only. Non-factual outputs are mostly 'the' or 'also'.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Modified attention for the factual-token-promoting heads.

conditions.value: hinted subset; factual target is a substring of the subject

rows.measure: Proportion of outputs predicting the factual token
rows.note: This is an output-rate result for prompts where the factual token is already present in the subject; it does not directly measure attention to that occurrence.
rows.check: This row is on counterfactual prompts. It measures the factual output rate when the fact is a substring of the subject, not suppression of a present token. It shows that boosting helps mainly when the fact is copyable, which is a different construct. There is no subset baseline.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Modified attention for the factual-token-promoting heads.

conditions.value: no-hint subset; factual target is not a substring of the subject

rows.measure: Proportion of outputs predicting the factual token
rows.note: The authors also state that the model predicted neither the factual nor the counterfactual token in 45% of no-hint cases.
rows.check: This is the same as r4 for the no-hint subset. It concerns whether the heads support factual recall, not copy suppression of a present token.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Measured relevant heads' contribution to the factual-versus-counterfactual logit difference across categorized dataset slices.
rows.measure: Head contribution to the logit difference between counterfactual and factual tokens
rows.value: figure only; the text states that subject and answer categories have a strong effect, and changing answer category has a greater effect than changing subject category
rows.note: The text describes category dependence for the GPT-2 heads responsible for the competition, including L10H7 among the heads of interest, but does not give a head-specific numeric result.
rows.check: The result is figure-only and not resolved for L10H7. The text says GPT-2's influential heads contribute significantly regardless of category, with strength varying by answer category. No L10H7 value can be read.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Modified random attention heads in the same layers as the heads of interest.
rows.value: The model mostly continued to output counterfactuals; the authors state that moderate changes significantly affected performance only when the heads of interest were modified.
rows.note: The authors describe very large alpha values as sometimes causing low-quality predictions that were neither target.
rows.check: This is a control (random heads) run on the original counterfactual prompts, not on the factual-repeat prompts of r1 and r2. It does not measure L10H7 and cannot carry a verdict by itself.

relationships.condition: GPT-2, L10H7 and L11H10 amplified jointly (alpha 5 and 10), prompts that state and then repeat the true fact
relationships.reason: Amplified heads suppress the factual token already present in the context, cutting factual output to below 90% and below 70% (r1, r2).
relationships.display_finding: Joint amplification at α = 5 and 10 suppressed the factual token already present in context, reducing factual output below 90% and 70%, respectively.

relationships.condition: Pythia-6.9B logit attribution across answer categories
relationships.reason: Based on the text (no row): L20H18 and others affect many categories negligibly, and SVD shows L20H18 encodes location and language. So the suppression role in Pythia is domain-specialized, not general.
relationships.display_finding: L20H18 and other heads had negligible effects across many answer categories, while singular value decomposition linked L20H18 to location and language.

relation.reason: The study directly compares general copy suppression with selective counterfactual suppression using its own interventions and results.

tranche.reason: Attention modification and factual-output rates test general copy suppression using a different method and measure from the original circuit and loss analysis.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. Domain specialization rests on attribution and OV SVD; the authors explicitly leave attention interventions by head and domain to future work, and report no uncertainty estimates for the main factual-prompt rates.

statements.correction: Section 4.4.2: negligible category contributions reported for L16H17, L19H31, L20H18, L21H7 and L24H5; factual-promoting heads examined by SVD include L21H7 and L20H18; L20H18 encodes location and language tokens.
statements.problem: The listed head group conflates the amplification experiment with the domain analysis; domain specialization is not established separately for L17H28 and L21H8.

statements.correction: Sections 4.2.1–4.2.2: GPT-2 robustness experiments; alpha 10 performs better for matching sentence structures, alpha 5 for differing structures. Section 4.3.2: Pythia-6.9B factual output varies with alpha and is below 70% at alpha 10 on factual prompts. Section 4.4.2: Pythia-6.9B head contributions vary by answer category.
statements.problem: The sentence-structure dependence of the best alpha is reported in the GPT-2 robustness experiment, not established for Pythia-6.9B.
